objectives: Run binary search over values you compute on demand, instead of a stored list.
Convert between a position in a flat list and a (row, column) in a grid.
Decide which searches need full sorted order and which need a different rule.

sections.heading: Intuition: binary search needs order, not a list
paragraphs: Binary search only ever asks two things: what's the value at index i, and is it smaller or bigger than what I want? It doesn't care whether that value comes from an array, a formula, or a grid, as long as the values go up as i goes up.
A grid can be read as one long list, row by row. In a grid with 3 columns, list position 5 is row 5 ÷ 3 = 1, column 5 mod 3 = 2. Going the other way, (row 1, column 2) is position 1 × 3 + 2 = 5.

callout.text: For a grid with c columns: position p is row p / c and column p % c (integer division). Cell (r, col) is position r · c + col.

diagram.description: A 2 by 3 grid numbered 0 to 5 row by row. Position 5 is row 1, column 2.

sections.heading: Baseline: look at every cell
paragraphs: Checking every cell of an m × n grid always works and takes O(m·n). Whether you can do better depends on how the grid is ordered, which is exactly what today's three problems vary.

sections.heading: Worked example: search values you compute
paragraphs: Is 49 in the list 0², 1², 2², ..., 10²? You could build the list, but you don't need to. value(i) = i·i can be computed whenever the search looks at index i, and it increases with i, so binary search works on it directly.
The code is the day 8 search with values[mid] replaced by mid * mid. The same idea lets you search a grid, a range of answers, or anything else where you can compute the value at a position.

sections.heading: Your turn: Search a 2D Matrix
paragraphs: Today's first medium. Each row of the grid is sorted, and each row's first value is greater than the previous row's last value. Return whether target is in the grid, in O(log(m·n)) time.

callout.text: Write out the grid from the problem's example as one list, row by row. What do you notice, and what does the key-idea box above let you do with it?

paragraphs: Today's second medium. Now each row is sorted left to right and each column top to bottom, but a row can start below the previous row's end. Return whether target is in the grid.

sections.heading: Your turn: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
paragraphs: Today's third medium. A sorted array of distinct values was rotated: [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7] might become [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]. Find the minimum in O(log n).

callout.text: The array isn't sorted, but binary search only needs a yes/no question that flips once. Draw [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2] as a graph and look for one.
callout.title: Where to start

sections.heading: Complexity and cautions
paragraphs: Binary search over a computed value costs O(log n) times the cost of computing one value. Computing i·i can overflow a 32-bit int for large i; use 64-bit math.
Converting positions with / and % is O(1), so treating an m × n grid as a flat list keeps searches at O(log(m·n)).

sections.heading: Before you finish
paragraphs: Try to answer each question before opening it.

checks.prompt: In a grid with 4 columns, which cell is position 9?
What two things does binary search need from the data?
checks.answer: A way to get the value at a position, and values that are in order, so one comparison rules out half.

checks.prompt: Why can't you binary search a grid that is sorted only by rows and columns as one flat list?
checks.answer: Read row by row, its values can go down between rows, so a comparison at mid doesn't rule out half.
